column1: # title: ENG-205 Sir Gawain Part 3 — 4 Main Ideas
The guide's offer to let Gawain flee
column2: On New Year's Day Gawain, secretly wearing the girdle, refuses the guide's offer to keep quiet if Gawain rides away, saying "I'd be christened a coward," so Gawain keeps his word and faces the Green Chapel even while relying on the girdle to save him.

At the Green Chapel the Green Knight feints once when Gawain flinches, holds back once when Gawain stands still, and only nicks Gawain's neck the third time, and the Green Knight later explains that the two harmless swings repay the two days Gawain honestly traded his winnings while the nick is for the third day, when "you strayed."

column1: The Green Knight's verdict on Gawain
column2: Revealing that he is Bertilak and sent his wife to test Gawain, the Green Knight calls Gawain "the most faultless fellow on earth," like a pearl beside a white pea, but says "it was loyalty that you lacked" because "you loved your own life," which shows the real test was in the castle all along and Gawain only partly failed it.

column1: Morgan le Fay's test of the Round Table
column2: Bertilak reveals that Morgan le Fay, Arthur's half sister and Gawain's aunt, sent him to Camelot in green "to put pride on trial" and test "what distinction and trust the Round Table deserves," so the whole adventure tested Arthur's court and chivalry itself, not only Gawain.

column1: The two meanings of the green girdle
column2: Ashamed, Gawain curses his "cowardice and covetousness" and wears the girdle home as "the symbol of sin" to humble his pride, but Arthur's court laughs and adopts green sashes as an honor, so the poem ends with Gawain humbled and reborn while readers still debate whether he failed or is the best of knights.
